name: list
title: List
description: A vertical stack of rows — contacts, settings, messages, files — each a ListItem, divided and edge-to-edge.

base.summary: The list draws almost nothing itself. The rows own their padding, their dividers and their states; the list owns only the surface they sit on and the space they cannot clip into.

tokens.background: inherited — the list takes the surface it is placed on, which is what lets it sit edge-to-edge in a page or inside a Sheet
tokens.padding-inline: space.0 — rows fill the width, for the reason SideNav's rows do: the whole row is the target
tokens.padding-block: space.0 — the recipe padded the block edges by focus.ring-width plus focus.ring-offset so the first and last rows' rings survived a scroll container; a row's ring is now drawn inside the row (gate 3, owner decision), so there is nothing to make room for, and padding would stop the first and last rows' state layers short of an inset list's corners
tokens.list-style: none, with role="list" restored — see the web and native decision

inset.summary: The grouped look: the list as a rounded surface inside the page's gutter, as in a settings screen.

tokens.overflow: clip, so the first and last rows' state layers take the container's corners — a row's focus ring is drawn inside the row, so the clip never cuts it

behavior.summary: A `<ul role="list">` of ListItems. No primitive and no keyboard model of its own: each interactive row is a link or a button in the normal tab order, which is what a list of rows is everywhere except inside a widget.

decisions.decision: It is a list, not a listbox, not a menu, not a nav
decisions.why: Four patterns look like a column of rows and announce four different things. A listbox is a single form control with a selection, one tab stop and arrow keys — choosing a row from a set is RadioGroup, or Select, or a checkbox per row, not this. A menu is a transient list of commands behind a trigger — that is Menu. A list of destinations that is the site's navigation is SideNav. This is the remaining case, and the commonest one in an app: a stack of independent things, each of which may open its own page or carry its own control, read in order with Tab moving from row to row.

decisions.decision: Dividers are on by default, and the rows draw them
decisions.why: Dense rows without a rule between them read as one block of text; CLAUDE.md's frame table already calls for lists that are 'edge-to-edge, divided'. Each row draws its own top rule except the first, so a list with conditional rows never shows a doubled or orphaned divider, and `dividers={false}` turns them off for a list whose rows are already separated by their own height.

decisions.decision: `appearance="inset"` is the only container variant, and it is not a Card
decisions.why: The grouped settings look — rows on a rounded surface inside the gutter — is common enough on mobile that every consumer would otherwise hand-roll it, and it is a property of the list rather than a wrapper around it. It is deliberately not a general-purpose Card: it holds rows and nothing else, and CLAUDE.md's rule against a hand-rolled `<div className="card">` still stands for everything that is not a list.

Unlike Tabs, there is no id wiring between parts to get wrong: a row stands alone, and its text, slots and control vary from row to row in ways a data shape would have to anticipate. Children keep ListItem's props as the one place a row is described, the same split Menu and MenuItem make.

A list where rows can be checked for a bulk action is a list of rows each carrying a Checkbox in `leading`, which composes from what exists. A list where exactly one row is the answer is a RadioGroup. A multi-select mode here would need `aria-multiselectable` and a listbox's keyboard model, which would turn this into the widget the first decision says it is not.

Rendering only the visible rows changes what is in the DOM, which changes what find-in-page, a screen reader's list count and Tab can reach. Those are solvable — `aria-setsize` and `aria-posinset` on each row — but they are a behaviour of their own and they belong in a primitive that has been through gate 1, not in a styling component.

decisions.decision: Pull-to-refresh is not part of List, and is not a component
decisions.why: It was proposed as a component and declined. On the web the browser already owns the gesture on the document scroller — Chrome on Android and Safari on iOS both reload the page on an overscroll — so a custom one has to disable that with `overscroll-behavior-y: contain` and replace a behaviour readers already know. It has no surface of its own beyond a Spinner, it binds to a scroll container rather than rendering anything, and on React Native it is not a component either: it is `RefreshControl`, passed to a `ScrollView` or `FlatList`'s `refreshControl` prop. Its non-gesture equivalent — a Refresh Button, or refreshing on focus — has to exist regardless, and that equivalent is what ships today. If installed PWAs (which lose the browser's gesture in standalone mode) make the gesture worth having, it is a `refreshing` / `onRefresh` pair on this component, mirroring FlatList's, backed by a new pointer-state primitive proposed through gate 1.

On the web it renders `<ul role="list">`, named by `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby` when given one. The explicit role is load-bearing: Safari removes list semantics from a list styled `list-style: none`, which is every list here, and without it VoiceOver stops announcing 'list, 12 items'. On React Native it renders a `View` with `accessibilityRole="list"` for short static lists. A long native list should be a `FlatList` — virtualization is not optional at a few hundred rows on a phone — so the native package is expected to take `data` and `renderItem` where the web takes `children`; that divergence is an open question for the native package's own gate 1. `className` is web-only. Swipe actions live on ListItem, and this component has no gesture of its own. Rata-drawn rows inside the core list views (decision N5): `View` or `FlatList` supplies the scrolling and the list semantics, and no OS table or list styling (UITableView, RecyclerView) is used. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

decisions.decision: A row's focus ring is drawn inside the row, so the list needs no block padding
decisions.why: Decided at gate 3, owner decision, docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md. ListItem draws its ring with a negative offset of focus.ring-offset plus focus.ring-width, so it never reaches the list's edges and neither a scroll container nor the inset appearance's `overflow: clip` can cut it. That removes the only reason for the block padding the gate-2 recipe gave the list, and the padding is space.0: kept, it would also stop the first and last rows' state layers short of an inset list's rounded corners, which the clip exists to give them.

children.summary: The rows: ListItem elements, in reading order.
use: ListItems, and nothing else at the top level.
dont: A heading or a paragraph between rows. A `<ul>` may contain only `<li>`; a section break is two Lists with a Heading between them.
children.a11y: Each ListItem is an `<li>`, so the list's item count is the number of rows a reader hears announced.

label.summary: Accessible name for the list, when no visible heading names it.
use: A list with no heading above it whose purpose is not obvious from its rows.
dont: Repeating a visible heading. Point at it with `labelledBy` instead, so the two cannot drift.

labelledBy.summary: Id of a visible element — usually the Heading above the list — that names it.
use: Every list with a heading directly above it.
dont: An id that is not on the page. A dangling reference names the list nothing, silently.

dividers.summary: Whether a rule is drawn between rows.
use: `false` for a short list of tall rows — each with an avatar and two lines — whose height already separates them.
dont: `false` on dense one-line rows. Without the rule they read as one paragraph.

appearance.summary: Edge-to-edge on the page's own surface, or grouped on a rounded surface inside the gutter.
use: `inset` for a settings screen, where each list is a group of related options under a heading.
dont: `inset` for a long feed or a search result. The container says 'this is a small fixed group', and a feed is neither.

className.summary: Extra classes on the `<ul>`, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: The margin the page wants around the list.
dont: Row padding or divider colour. Those are ListItem's, and a list that restyles its rows from outside is two places deciding one thing.

usage.when: A handful of related options on a mobile settings screen, under a heading.
usage.example:
<Heading level={2} id="notifications">Notifications</Heading>
<List labelledBy="notifications" appearance="inset">
  <ListItem trailing={<Switch label="Email" labelHidden checked={email} onCheckedChange={setEmail} />}>Email</ListItem>
  <ListItem href="/settings/quiet-hours" description="10 pm – 7 am">Quiet hours</ListItem>
</List>
usage.notes: The heading names the list through `labelledBy`, so it is read 'Notifications, list, 2 items'. The first row holds a control and is not itself clickable; the second is a link. Both are normal rows in one list.

usage.case: A feed of things, each opening its own page
usage.when: Messages, files, orders — a long column where each row leads somewhere.
usage.notes: `plain` and divided, edge-to-edge. Each row is one link, so Tab moves from order to order and a screen reader's links list reads the titles alone.

usage.case: Reaching for the wrong component: picking one
usage.when: The rows are the options of a question, and the reader chooses one of them.
usage.example:
<List label="Shipping speed">
  <ListItem onClick={() => setSpeed("standard")}>Standard</ListItem>
  <ListItem onClick={() => setSpeed("express")}>Express</ListItem>
</List>
usage.notes: Don't. Nothing here says which one is chosen or that only one can be. That is a RadioGroup, which announces the choice, holds the answer, and submits it with the form.
